I use lambdas to expose the real functionality and hide any error handling and tracing.

Most software has 70%-80% error handling or logging functionality, so the real functionality is buried in unimportant code.

By using Lamba''s you bring back the real functionality to the surface and bury the logging and error recovery a layer lower. When you look at my code it looks surprisingly simple but it does pack a big punch that does not distracts you.

I don't think I am at a point where I can appreciate that style of coding. I'm even having trouble envisioning how you would use lambdas efficiently. Couldn't you just create a class with all of the error handling and logging methods and then just subclass it to get at the essence of the desired functionality?

That subclassing would create more code and making your code even more complex.

Most people use lambda's in LINQ statements. That gives the impression that it is more complex, and I agree it makes code harder to read. I rarely use LINQ, only if the code is more readable.

I tend to use code like this (not exactly just to get an idea)


Process((x)==> {
 ...
 DoSomething().
 var isFailed=DoSomethingElse()
 ...
 return IsFailed;
}

DoProcess() is one method that can wrap the start of the tracing, the error handling the logging, everything a layer deep. I can reuse the same DoProcess() for many different methods in the same class.

DoProces will be the most complex part in your code, but the functional part in the code will become incredibly easy to read, debug and test.

I am a C# developer not Python but this is how I do use Lambdas (very rought draft).

public void Funtion1(){
 Process((x)==> {
 Method1();
 }
}

public void Funtion2(){
 Process((x)==> {
 Method2();
 }
}

public void Funtion3(){
 Process((x)==> {
 Method3();
 }


public void DoProcess(lambda aaa) {
 Trace.WriteLine("Start method")
 try {
 aaa();
 } catch (exception e) {
 Trace.WriteLine("Exception"+e.Message)
 }

 Trace.WriteLine("End method")
 }
}

My takeaway from this article is that lambdas still seem to be pointless in Python unless you just really like using them.

I've always felt that they were awkward to fit in to my coding style, because I always go for what I believe to be the more Pythonic solution to a given problem. This usually involves comprehensions, generators, and reusable named functions.

The only example I can see that had merit was the one about callbacks. Using a lambda there can be handy if all you want to do is print something, but you can just define that in a method and have that be called. For that particular example, defining a method would be easier to maintain if you wanted to add additional functionality later (maybe something like format the text based on time of day) or modify the output string.

I'm not saying lambdas are bad. It's just that I've never seen a compelling reason to use it. As for the article, it had good examples and is formatted nicely. Thanks for sharing.

Lambda always keep coming up, so it doesn't hurt to know about them. However I doubt I would really use them unless someone said, "use a lambda function here.

Birmingham MP Jess Phillips recently laughed in parliament at the mere idea of a debate focussing on men's issues coinciding with International Men's Day. An article discussing this was posted to /v/news by myself.

Afterwards, she reports receiving a barrage of rape and death threats which reduced her to tears. The media ran with this (as expected) reporting how resilient and brave she is and how she's mostly concerned for her children rather then herself. A list of outlets is available here, and there's a definite theme to the articles; damsel in distress being targeted by anonymous internet trolls. sigh

A few things piqued my curiosity here.

Interestingly, when someone asked for proof of the abuse, she produced one tweet. It contained 2 downvoted comments from voat itself. These were horrible things to say but it was hardly a "barrage" or "torrent" as being reported. Don't get me wrong, there was criticism and insults in the thread, but again, a few people on voat calling her a cunt is not a pandemic (and arguably true IMO).

According to Sky News, she reported these to the police When receiving threats, police advise not to publicise them as to not draw attention to the trolls. Anyone who's ever been harassed online knows this. Therefore, she should have refused as retweeting anything would directly contradict police advice. This implies to me she hasn't reported it at all (pure speculation here, as far as I know there's no way to check with Westmidlands police if a report has been filed).

Also, from a language viewpoint, neither comment were technically threats. From a legal perspective, the language in a threat requires intention. Meaning the uses of the words "should" and "would" as opposed to "I will" make it a grey area whether these were legally threats. Horrible things to say definitely, but the UK only has precedent of convicting when the threats are direct as in the case of Caroline Criado Perez. The Bahar Mustafa case may change this soon but her hyperbolic tweets could still be considered directly threatening to a group of people. Legally, anonymous trolling is a notoriously murky area and would be hard take to court as it stands. However, I am far from a legal expect so take everything I've said as potentially incorrect.

Also, isn't it very unprofessional of a politician to be calling people "pricks" on twitter?

In bad reporting news, most places claimed she was the victim of twitter abuse (I don't use twitter so cannot comment here) and the voat examples have mostly been presented as though they were tweets themselves. The Mirror is the only major outlet I could find which said otherwise and they claimed the comments came from Reddit! I'm certainly not implying voat is somehow missing out by going unmentioned but isn't checking sources before publishing journalism 101? Kudos for trying though, I guess.

These are purely my observations though, if I'm completely wrong let me know!
